Sophistic Humor and Social Change: Overcoming Identification with the Aggressor

Mark Wright

Mark Wright

Mark Wright   Associate Professor in the English Department of Tsuda College. He specializes in uncovering and evaluating intersections between rhetorical and psychological theory. In 1996, he received the Emerging Scholar Award from the Kenneth Burke Society for his work on the psychological theoretical bases of Kenneth Burke's theories of identification and persuasion.

Psychological barriers to social change represent rhetorical challenges. The critic hoping to contribute to social change must uncover discursive strategies for overcoming psychological barriers. Ideally, those strategies must be teachable to students or clients for academic critics to make positive contributions to the public sphere. On another level, if we agree with Maurice Charland that “rhetoric's high card in postmodern social theory” is that it “conceives of the audience as a ‘capacity to respond’ that forms the horizon for a determination of the good and for proper praxis,” then we must ask whether that high card may be played when an audience has a severely diminished “capacity to respond” (“Finding” 73).

As a response to those challenges, this essay will explore the implications for rhetoric of the psychoanalytic idea of “sophistic joking.” Using the examples of comedians Mort Sahl and Dick Gregory, it will show how sophistic joking can overcome identification with the aggressor, a powerful barrier to social change. After exploring this barrier, it will explain Freud's notion of sophistic joking and explore Sahl's and Gregory's uses of this discursive form to overcome identification with the aggressor. Finally, it will consider some of the limitations of sophistic joking.

Identification with the Aggressor as a Barrier to Social Change

Identification with the aggressor was first described in a psychoanalytic context by Sigmund Freud. In The Interpretation of Dreams, Freud described a dream in which he placed himself in the position of one who had the power to deny him a professorship. Also in the dream, he used his position to denounce his uncle and his friend. Rather than wait passively for the appointment, in the dream Freud took over an active role, and some of the cruelty of the persons currently in those positions, as well. Further, in Beyond the Pleasure Principle, Freud noted that often when a child has suffered some invasive procedure at the hands of the doctor or dentist, the same procedure is soon inflicted on other children in play (16).

James Glass

James Glass

James Glass   Professor of Government and Politics at the University of Maryland, College Park. He has published extensively in the fields of Political Psychology, Psychiatry, and Political Theory. That any Jewish resistance occurred during the Holocaust was extraordinary, given the power of the German assault on Jewish bodies and minds and the devastation produced by ghettoization. Yet, essential to the existence of resistance was the capacity of resistors to transcend the radical inversion of meaning and value imposed by the German occupation and German racist policies. Resistance occurred against a backdrop of group psychosis. I would like to address the power of psychosis on the group level and its relationship to psychosis in the individual. Group madness and individual madness are quite different, but there is one very frightening similarity: the power of perception (delusion) to literally transform reality to conform with the projections of the subject.

For the psychotic subject, reality is what delusion defines as reality; for the group, reality is what the group ideological consensus defines as truth and necessity. And in the case of the Germans, what reality defined as necessity was the Jewish menace in radically distorting biological and genetic reality to make life untenable. The Jew as an absolute and mortal danger had to be physically eliminated before the German cultural group could be assured of safety. These allusions appear continually in German policy and propaganda statements. It is this kind of psychological universe that the resistor was forced to confront, fight, and overcome: the Jew as evil threatening the very foundations of the Aryan future.

The resistor, then, comes to represent and affirm an historical sanity, a value embedded in history and the history of ethics: the refusal of the premises of mass murder and the murder of an identified and marked group simply because this group exists. That assumption that the Other must die because the Other exists has no standing in an ethical history that grants dignity to human life. And when the resistor refused either physically or spiritually the Germans' view of reality, that refusal embraced an affirmation and sanity that German rage could not touch or destroy.

On Teaching Psychoanalysis

Susan Varney

Susan Varney

Susan Varney   Graduate student in literature at SUNY Buffalo, where she is completing a dissertation tentatively entitled, “Virtue in Chains: Liberty, Equality, Sexual Difference.” She has published articles on British modern literature as well as feminist and psychoanalytic theory.

As you may recall, one of the ways Freud classified psychoanalysis (in “Analysis Terminable and Interminable”) was as an “‘impossible’ profession in which one can be sure beforehand of achieving unsatisfying results.” Psychoanalysis was, he wagered, in some way comparable both to education and to government whose status as “impossible” has been known for much longer. Since I have spent a good deal of time over the last few years considering—attempting both to learn and to teach—the theoretical overlap between psychoanalysis and politics, this insight of Freud's is never very far from my thoughts.

If each field taken on its own terms is “impossible,” what are we to understand as the aim in the teaching of psychoanalysis and politics? For surely impossibility is another way of recognizing a certain lack or incompleteness of knowledge inherent to the system of thought itself, and if this is the case, then the question is not simply one of pedagogy but, in fact, reflects directly back onto the theory underpinning Freud's point concerning psychoanalysis' “impossibility.” For Freud what is clearly at stake is not only the transmission of a piece of knowledge but the imparting of an impossible knowledge, the transmission of a system of thought within which the hole or rupture in knowledge can itself come to the fore. It is only in the relation—or more precisely the impasse—between knowledge and “impossible knowledge” that the workings of the unconscious itself come to light. The problem that Freud then faces, and we in our turn, is how to teach a “knowledge” that is, in effect, only in absentia, that is as a lack or impossibility in knowledge.

When approached directly the question of an impossible knowledge becomes itself unreadable, inconceivable, and it is for this reason that we need both supporting institutions (such as the International Psychoanalytic Association) and signature myths (from seduction theory, to Oedipus, to the primal horde) in order to facilitate its transmission. They make order out of relative chaos and, in the latter case at least, provide a framework within which a psychoanalytic understanding of the costs of such order can begin to take shape. The Oedipus myth is, of course, all about an impossible knowledge, and those who come to Sophocles' tale via Freud are urged to take note of all the various effects that this elusive knowledge precipitates, the “order” and system to which it gives rise. But so much for theory. The institution of psychoanalysis presents us with another situation entirely, another—I would suggest, entirely unanalytic—relation to knowledge, and it is this with which I am specifically concerned here.

I have been coming to Bulgaria fairly frequently for nearly a decade and am in close and regular contact by email. I have felt honored to be asked to come here and then asked again. I am particularly pleased to be honored by you today. Thank you.

I am far from being an expert on your country, much less on the other countries in the former Soviet bloc, but I have always been interested in them. I used to listen secretly to Radio Moscow on short wave as a boy in Texas, fearing that I would one day be arrested for doing so, such was the paranoid atmosphere of that time. It was a time when we suffered virulent McCarthyist anti-Communist witch hunts, especially in Texas. When I eventually visited Russia in the early 1970s, I was assured that there was every reason to feel worried about human rights there. We were followed, spied on, and reported on, and women sought me out in order to compromise me.

I was told in no uncertain terms by Russian scholars that things had been and still were awful for academics as well as everyone else. For example, in biology and the history of biology it was fatal to question the pseudo-science of Lysenkoism. (Lest we be too complacent about this blatant undermining of science, I remind you that obscurantism never dies: in the American state of Kansas the teaching of evolution in the schools has in recent weeks been made very difficult by the Board of Education, and creationists are making similar inroads on Darwinian science in other American states.) When I was later close to the daughter of the former head of the Soviet Writers' Union, who became a colleague of mine at Cambridge, she told me dreadful things, so dreadful that her father had killed himself in the wake of Kruschev's revelations at the Twentieth Party Conference. She was very graphic in her descriptions of the hardships people experienced in the Soviet Union. I am sorry to say that she was herself so damaged by events in her childhood that she killed herself in London some years later.

To the Editor

The recent APCS conference on “Social Symptoms” brought together psychoanalytic thinkers from a diversity of perspectives, although the dominant paradigm present at the conference was (and has always been) clearly Lacanian. Listening to Elisabeth Young-Bruehl's post-conference comments both last year and this year, I wanted to reflect on what the difficulties feeling a part of this conference are for me, a psychoanalytic thinker from another paradigm. I personally do not have a problem with the difficult language or the creation of new language characteristic of the Lacanian paradigm. What at times makes the conference less than comfortable for me are two things: the presumption on the part of many speakers that the Lacanian paradigm is psychoanalysis, and a particular spirit in which Lacan is all too often invoked.

The first panel I attended featured Jon Brenkman, Tim Dean, and Drucilla Cornell. Brenkman was discussing the lack of fit between social critique and psychoanalysis; psychoanalysis was equated with Lacan. His argument suggested to me that there may not be a good fit between Lacanian theory and social criticism (although I later heard a few papers that cast doubt on this proposition), but, in equating psychoanalysis and Lacan, he buried the possibility that some of the many other versions of psychoanalysis that exist might be better equipped to address social symptoms. Although I am sure arrogance was not Brenkman's intention, the equation of Lacan and psychoanalysis leaves the non-Lacanian feeling excluded and condescended to. This feeling recurred when Drucilla Cornell opened her remarks with an anecdote in which she was telling colleagues at a conference on game theory that the following week she would be attending a Lacan conference. This is not a Lacan conference, my inner relational analytic voice protested.

Tim Dean's contribution helped me formulate the second source of my discomfort at APCS conferences. Dean spoke of alternative ways to approach a text besides the usual symptomatic approach. As a psychoanalytic feminist, I heard in this talk a lot of resonances with what many feminists who challenge the doer-done to model of subject-object relations have talked about in their work (Jessica Benjamin is one example). I wondered why some of this work was not mentioned, but that is a secondary issue. Primary is the recognition that it is not the difficulty of Lacanian language that causes discomfort and a feeling of exclusion, but rather it is the spirit in which Lacan and Lacanian theory is approached. Many speakers approach Lacan as a thinker whose concepts can help us make sense of the social world, but many more approach Lacan as an authority who always gets it right and who, in the last instance, always said it first. The papers and comments I find exciting and welcoming might, for example, have racial issues or other social symptoms in the foreground and Lacan in the background shedding light on the problem; here, some concept in Lacanian theory is helping the author make sense of a contemporary problem. These kinds of papers make me want to learn more about Lacan. On the other hand, the comments and papers I find off-putting have as their central concern not social symptoms but reverence for, even fetishization of, Lacan. In Kohutian language, Lacan here appears as a self-object, a means of stabilizing the speaker's self (in Lacanian language perhaps the equivalent is Lacan as object a). I write up these reflections because I think that APCS wants to foreground social change. One of the most important ways to work on social change is to address the type of relations we establish with texts, with masters, and with each other.

Introduction

This paper is an attempt to offer some insight into the senseless violence that has been occurring among adolescent boys in suburban America. By exploring the cases of Eric Harris and Dylan Klebold, the youths who stormed into their high school in April 1999 and shot and killed thirteen classmates in addition to themselves, I will consider the intra-psychic nature of violent children. A crucial element is shame, which Lynd defines as “a wound to one's self-esteem, a painful feeling or sense of degradation excited by the consciousness of having done something unworthy of one's previous idea of one's own excellence” (23). It is the feeling of being in a painful situation in which disdain of others is experienced, and at its center, an acute awareness of self. I use Harris and Klebold as examples in the hope that my speculative thinking about them will elucidate what is happening in the minds of other potentially violent boys. Shame involves the feeling of the entire self as negative or inferior, and is experienced when a destructive condition is present, when normal defenses cannot be used for some reason, or when guilty or self-abusive tendencies occur.

Shame: A Feeling of Negative Self-Worth

The actual feeling of shame involves the consciousness that the self is inferior, incompetent, and small. Without respect and proper treatment from those around him, a shame-prone person is vulnerable to self-blame and self-hatred. As such, he feels inadequate and unwanted, and experiences his self-esteem, well-being, and security as under attack. Shame involves a vicious cycle, as these feelings of inadequacy prevent him from presenting himself positively to others, leaving him vulnerable to further abuse and neglect.

Feelings associated with shame—normal or debilitating—are clear and painful because they increase a sense of self-consciousness. We are made more aware of traits that are central to our identities. These are traits that we mean to keep concealed from others, and more importantly, from ourselves. Although shame can lead to a positive experience of revelation and awareness, it is more likely to highlight our fragility and lack of self-esteem. Moments of shame evoke an awareness of the fragility of the conditions upon which hopes and aspirations are based. These moments make us realize how easily and quickly our desires may disappear. Further, we may also recognize with deep pain that our desires will ultimately be experienced as unfulfilled, even if they are satisfied (Goldberg).

In the aftermath of the recent school shootings, communities and the media alike have been searching for “answers” to the question of why young white males in suburban neighborhoods have been massacring their classmates. Some look to the parents who should have known what was happening, the difficult social environment of high school, or authorities who failed to act decisively. For example, in the wake of the Columbine shootings, Newsweek suggested that it was the fault of the police: “the sheriff's office had failed to act decisively on explicit threats made by Harris that foreshadowed the massacre” (“Beyond” 32). Conservatives blame Hollywood for its depiction of violence, while liberals blame gun companies for the lack of control over gun sales. Jonathan Alter, writing for Newsweek, encapsulates both of these critiques: “Simply meeting with gun and entertainment executives will accomplish little; individuals must be named and shamed” (59). While Alter wants to see individuals held accountable for school shootings, William Bennett, during a Senate commerce committee meeting addressing violence in Hollywood films and their influence on society, wants to see individual films held accountable. He explains, “Surely we can agree upon some meaningful distinctions here, between [the violence in] Casino and Saving Private Ryan, between The Basketball Diaries and Clear and Present Danger” (qtd. in Jenkins 21). Rather than blaming Hollywood for society's violence, however, we can instead look to Hollywood for some answers to the seemingly elusive question of where to put the blame. As we shall see, Hollywood films make clear what no one else has brought up when discussing these school shootings: the link between violence and masculinity.

When generalizing in his Violence: Reflections on a National Epidemic about who commits the most violence in America, James Gilligan says, “Violence is primarily men's work; it is carried out more frequently by men; and it is about the maintenance of ‘manhood’ “ (16). To me, as to Gilligan, the role that violence plays in creating and sustaining masculinity and femininity is its primary function. It is no surprise then that boys in their adolescence—the transition between boyhood and manhood—might see violence as a way to leave their mark on the world. Although no one surrounding the recent teen shootings mentions “manhood,” it is nonetheless the kernel of what is at stake. To understand the link between violence and masculinity and the recent teen shootings—I will look most specifically at the Columbine case—we must first consider the general interrelations of masculinity and violence. Violence is not simply equal to masculinity; instead, the two have a distinct and multifaceted relationship to each other, operating at three different, though related, levels. First, and most basically, violence acts as a signifier of masculinity; second, violence is a reaction to a loss of masculinity; and third, violence serves as the object of an economic exchange between men. If we grasp the full complexity of the relationship between violence and masculinity, it will become apparent the extent to which the violence of Columbine—and the other shootings that presage and echo it—has its genesis in the ideas and ideals of masculinity that continue to inform contemporary American culture.

According to a review of Edmund Morris's memoir of President Ronald Reagan, there was an important difference between Ronald Reagan and Bill Clinton in their orientation toward the truth. Clinton had a reputation for telling lies, while Reagan was unable to distinguish lies from what he believed to be true. Reviewer Steven Weisman reports, “[T]he difference [between fact and fiction] clearly did not matter to Reagan. His world was famously populated with welfare ‘queens’ who did not exist, with trees that caused pollution…. Reagan wasn't lying, because he believed what he said, even after being told that it was false” (7). Weisman concludes that Ronald Reagan lived in a world of his own fictions, but he will no doubt go down in history as “a giant who reflected the Zeitgeist of his era and hastened its destiny” (8).

Reagan is indeed a reflection of the Zeitgeist of our era, if we see this era as one where the lie no longer serves to prop up (and shield us from) the truth; where there is not so much the exposing of the father as impostor (for all fathers turn out to be impostors), but rather the loss of the “appearance” of an authority in the big Other.1 According to Slavoj Žižek and others, in this stage of late capitalist development there has been a shift in our symbolic structure, which has recast the subject as an opaque being in an endlessly reflexive world; he is “more than ever caught in an inexorable compulsion that effectively runs his life” (Ticklish 354). We have, according to Žižek been “colonized by reflexivity,” by the endless contingency of choice and scrutiny over all aspects of life, from proper forms of seduction to daily eating habits (Ticklish 336).

The shift we detect is a movement away from the virtual fictions of the symbolic toward imaginary simulacra of virtuality. In this shift and in this indeterminacy of the subject, symptoms emerge in a world of “acephalic” knowledge. Here the ways that are sought to avoid confrontation with the truth paradoxically work to help construct the very structure that hollows us out and makes us uncanny, even to ourselves. In these conditions, the authentic Act of re-setting one's global coordinates, of traversing the fundamental fantasy, seems more difficult than ever, for we have constructed, without our awareness, an automatic headless world that is pulsing onward, divorced from our intentions and our ability to recognize its effects. This is not to say that we ever really had control in the form of intentions and effects, but rather that now we live in a type of “risk society,” where there is no balance of a middle ground, where for many, the anxiety of possible catastrophic consequences of acts, of not knowing how to “freely” choose among infinite possibilities, produces extreme anxiety (Žižek, Ticklish 338).

In the 1950s and 1960s violence in westerns would often begin with a cowboy asserting that he didn't like the way a stranger looked at him. At Columbine High School, Klebold and Harris were violent, we are told, because they were treated as outcasts and “looked upon” with veiled or outright contempt. In Washington, D.C. last year more than 15 African American teenagers were shot because their shooters felt they were not being treated with respect by a person outside their gang. In all these acts of violence, the attacker and the victim belong to different membership groups, and the very act of a recognition of outsider status seems sufficient to generate feelings of discomfort and violent aggression.

If lack of recognition can fuel violence among gang members, the reverse is also true. The sheer need for group recognition can also motivate violence. In the “great” epics of Western culture Greek, Roman, and Anglo-Saxon heroes talk about war as a way of winning recognition. War is justified, in the rhetoric of the sagas anyway, not on the basis of some real material reward gained, but on the basis of the honor, admiration, or recognition it brings. Achilles, for example, speaks to Agamemnon: “I for my part did not come here for the sake of Trojan spearmen, to fight against them, since they are nothing to me; but for your sake … we followed you, to do your favour …, to win your honor and Menelaos'.” The great slaughter outside the gates of Troy, Achilles reveals, is not done for the trophies of war, women, and armor, but for honor. And the trophies of war, so carefully described by Homer, are valuable not as material objects, but as reminders of the admiration and recognition given the heroes. In the Anglo-Saxon world, when Beowulf comes to the great hall of Heorot, he tells the king that he seeks to win honor by taking on a difficult task. He risks his life because he craves the recognition and memory of a tribal group. It is as if “life” itself were not primarily biological, but symbolic, present more forcefully in ritualized acts of signification than in the body.

In this brief and by necessity oversimplified discussion I want to first present some basic concepts from British object relations theorists that can help expand and contrast Lacan's and Althusser's ideas on recognition and interpellation. I will take into account Robert Samuels's carefully articulated summary of Lacan's theories of recognition. Second, I will elaborate these ideas in reference to the recent episodes of school violence as discussed by Thomas J. Catlaw. In doing this I am attempting to move between Lacan and Althusser and Bion and Winnicott in looking at these events. And finally, I will add my own thoughts from my own developing concepts of group work where I use both Lacan's theory and object relations thinking.

Bion argues that thinking develops out of emotions and sensory experiences that are processed by the mother as a container. According to Bion, the subject learns to “contain” its feelings of aggression as a result of its early pattern of relating to the mother. Before the use of language, a number of developmental tasks take place in a dialogue of recognition between the baby and the mother. In this process, the mother serves as a container who receives the baby's early sensory impressions (beta-elements, similar to Lacan's real). If the containment process is fortunate, beta-elements develop into alpha-elements, or sense and emotional experiences that later serve as visual and imagistic experience. Alpha elements, thus, can become part of dream thoughts, unconscious thinking, dreams, and memories.

What is contained is influenced by the baby's capacity to tolerate frustration—in other words, by genetic factors. Additionally Bion speaks of the beta-element screen.

It is on the face of it a daunting task to respond from the somewhat peripheral perspective of group dynamics, and in a small space, to the subtle and powerful analysis that Thomas Catlaw offers in his essay on recognition and school violence. Indeed, it would probably not be possible to do so sensibly save for the support provided by the Samuels and Giraldo pieces that accompany it. The helpful context Samuels sets enables me to utilize aspects of all of three of Lacan's perspectives on recognition—in the Imaginary, the Real, and the Symbolic—without elaboration and without seeming inconsistent. In a similar way, Giraldo's essay explicates a critically important concept relating to group functioning and does so clearly enough that I can invoke it by reference only.

Group facilitation provides a revealing context for seeing the power of Lacanian concepts as they apply at the level of social process. Groups are a microcosmic social order, and as such, provide a laboratory that displays the interplay of the Lacanian registers as they function to constellate the human subject—or fail to do so.

Subjectivity must be understood in terms of the type of Symbolic Order (at present it is late-modernism) that is hegemonic at a given moment.

“Technically speaking the Satanists,” Simen Midgaard wrote in 1995, “form a Christian sect” (Moynihan 345). Because Satan “is as Christian as Jesus” (345), “you can't believe in the Devil and still fight Christendom,” Michael Moynihan lucidly comments (256). In other words, adults who fear that youth who turn to Satan turn away from Christianity fail to see that in fact they remain deep within the fold. Whatever Satanism might signify in an individual case, as a cultural symptom it does not represent a break with, but rather an inversion of Christian norms and ideals: “youthful Satanism is an extreme breed of Christianity where serenity, truth and honesty exchange gods for their opposite” (345). The “youthful” Satanist exchanges the officially, perhaps unbearably, loving Holy Family of Christianity for a darkly parodic anti-family: it is widely understood that, when Anton Lavey, founder of the Church of Satan, advised his followers to sacrifice thousands of children daily, he was humorously recommending masturbation.

Children and adolescents do not invent their religions, nor design the symbolic order(s) in which they seek to play a meaningful role; rather, they inherit them and, like their parents and others, use them to configure or re-configure oedipal constellations. Freud thought religion was “patently infantile” (74), derived “from the infant's helplessness and the longing for the father aroused by it” (72). If the religious beliefs of an adult belie his infantile feelings, what do the religious beliefs of a young person express? Perhaps, given the intersubjective nature of family romance, they reveal certain repressed feelings his adult intimates have about him—feelings not his own (and to which adults respond with the uncanny horror of unavowed self-recognition). Christianity, Americas unofficial official religion, provides us with our paradigmatic family, comprising one “enormously exalted father” (Freud 74), one receptive virgin mother, and one perfect sacrificial son. Satanism provides thousands if not millions of people, individually and collectively, with the fantasy of an alternative jouissance that can be interpreted as the refusal to identify with the role of sacrificed son, to identify instead with an unsublimated individualistic anti-father who takes sadistic pleasure in the sacrifice of others, children especially.1

Editor's Column

Adolescent Violence and Identity Vulnerability

Mark Bracher

Mark Bracher

Mark Bracher  

Adolescent violence in the United States—which the Columbine school massacre of April 20, 1999, forced the public to recognize as serious and ubiquitous—is a social problem that cries out for psychoanalytic solutions. A psychodynamic perspective is crucial, first of all, for understanding what causes adolescent violence and why it—especially in its severest forms, homicide and suicide—has increased so dramatically in recent decades and is so much greater in the U. S. than in all other Western nations. A psychodynamic perspective is crucial, in addition, for understanding and addressing the causes of our collective failure to acknowledge the seriousness of the problem. And such a perspective is also invaluable for understanding why, to the extent that we have recognized the seriousness of the problem and understood what causes it and how to prevent it, we have as a society failed in large measure to act upon this knowledge and implement effective preventive measures.

Magnitude of the Problem

The scope and significance of adolescent violence in the United States today can be indicated by a few statistics. First, youth are disproportionately involved in interpersonal violence, both as victims and as perpetrators. In recent years, youth between the ages of 12 and 24 committed roughly half of all crimes of violence, fatal and nonfatal, reported in the U. S. (Hamburg 32). Adolescents up to the age of 21 commit about one-fourth of the 23,000 homicides that occur in the U. S. each year (Garbarino 6). One survey found that nearly one-fourth of students in the U. S. reported carrying a weapon to school during the previous month (Hamburg 36).

In addition, the involvement of American youth in violence has been increasing: between 1985 and 1990, the rate of adolescent homicides increased by 168 percent, and between 1965 and 1993, the average age of killers in the U. S. decreased from 33 to 27 (7). The same is true of suicide. Each year about 2,300 youth aged 18 or younger take their own lives, four times the rate of 1950 (Garbarino 9).

The explosion of interest in trauma theory among literary and cultural critics would seem to confirm Kirby Farrell's claim that the United States is a “post-traumatic culture.” While not a new diagnosis—Elaine Showalter reads the epidemiology of United States culture and calls it “history”; while others, like Robert Hughes, label it a “culture of complaint”—Farrell asks how trauma, a concept invented a century ago, has become a central trope in the cultural imagination of the late twentieth century. His answer, Post-Traumatic Culture: Injury and Interpretation in the Nineties, is a capacious and, at times, deeply engaging analysis of an archive that spans two continents and several centuries.

The book's structural trope is to juxtapose fin de siècle Britain and 1990 America, calling the resemblance between the decades the “return of the repressed” (29). The figure of St. George, with whom Kirby begins the book, is read, for example, as an early figure of traumatic heroism, a fallen martyr who, in the 1890s, symbolically justifies British imperialism, and who returns, nearly a century later, as a warrior-saint capable of saving America from the “evil empire” in the likes of Rambo and Ronald Reagan. Indeed, the iconography of St. George and the “mood of traumatic rescue” he inspires permeates several of Farrell's astute analyses, from the politics of Vietnam and Reaganomics to the film Pretty Woman. The vocabulary of trauma in Post-traumatic Culture is, in other words, as ubiquitous as it is equivocal. Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder—a familiar clinical diagnosis for Vietnam veterans—becomes more sinister in its symptoms as Farrell demonstrates, for example, how the nation's sense of “traumatic victimization” in the post-war years could come to justify the traumatic economic policies of the Reagan years. Nosce Teipsum (Read Thyself) As the sub-title explains, The Disposition of the Subject: Reading Adorno's Dialectic of Technology is a study of Adorno's concept of technology. The topic is well selected, since it would be hard to locate a more crucial idea in the whole of his oeuvre. Anyone interested in Adorno's thought would want to welcome the project.

The author—Erik Krakauer —proceeds in four chapters, with an epilogue. The first is a discussion of the Dialectic of Enlightenment, and claims that in this volume Adorno “discovered a dark side to the Enlightenment;” the technological mastery of nature has “proven to be both pernicious as well as salubrious;” the second chapter argues that technological rationality is not only an epistemological conundrum but “a social and political problem as well;” the third chapter shows that technological rationality is disrupted by Adorno's negative dialectics. This thesis is especially developed in the fourth chapter, in which Krakauer extracts from Adorno's texts the surprising admission—for anyone who has so much as mowed a lawn—that “technology is primarily a language.” Once Krakauer has established this idea, he segues directly into boiler plating about the metaphysics of representation, and how the self and its autarchic claims are an effect of this metaphysical tendency inherent in all language. However familiar these ideas, what catches the eye here is that it is Adorno, the philosopher of a dialectical reasoning generally held anathema to post-structuralism, who is now said to provide a type of destabilizing rhetoric that “has much in common with Paul de Man's deconstructive reading” (13-14). Krakauer especially discerns de Manian practice in Adorno's much reputed use of foreign—Greek, Latin, French and English—words in his German texts. Their foreignness destroys significiative textual closure and—says Krakauer—heals the wounds first inflicted on nature by the metaphysical self. It is in enthusiasm for these foreign words in the struggle against metaphysics that Krakauer builds the credo quia with which the book concludes: “Language which listens to itself, words which discover the foreignness of words, slash the fundamental speculative I…. The word as trace represents nothing, nor does it maintain or preserve anything…. Only language can dispel the effects of language, only language can deconstruct the language of metaphysics and poison poisonous or pernicious language. Only the surgery of writing can heal what grows malignantly from the site of previous surgery” (179).

In Victorian studies, as in other fields of literary and cultural studies, the predominance of various kinds of historicism has tended to lead to the devaluation of psychoanalytic approaches to literature. Christopher Lane's Burdens of Intimacy argues for the continued importance and relevance of a psychoanalytic approach, claiming that nineteenth-century literature's understanding of the unconscious “repeatedly challenges a strictly materialist understanding of identity” (xi). More specifically, he argues against the notion of psychic life as “an effect of cultural pressure or historical events” (xviii) and for the ways in which “desire conveys and masks internal difficulties” (xi), chiefly “the insurmountable division between consciousness and the unconscious that belies all hope of unifying personal objectives” (xiii). Thus, rather than seeing the cultural regulation of sexuality as the primary force thwarting desire between men in Victorian novels, Lane uses psychoanalysis to demonstrate the complexities and ambiguities of desire and identification. For him “sexual desire is not constructed as such, but is instead the point of identificatory failure” (xiii).

Lane makes his argument through seven chapters of eloquent and subtle readings of nineteenth- and twentieth-century literature. Chapter One, on Edward Bulwer-Lytton's Pelham, examines the revisions of this novel made between 1828 and 1840. The revisions tend to masculinize an initially effeminate dandy figure. Rather than reading them purely as the effect of increasing cultural intolerance of effeminacy, Lane focuses on the novel's critical engagement with the very process of repression itself, and the impossibility built into that process. Chapter Two, on the poet Algernon Charles Swinburne's novel, Lesbia Brandon, argues for Swinburne's understanding of the unconscious and the ways in which it complicates his understanding of desire. Chapter Three, on Olive Schreiner's The Story of an African Farm, is one of the strongest in the book, pointing out the tension between Schreiner's communitarian vision on the one hand, and the sexual fantasies that produce her heroine's masochism and the effeminization of some of her male characters on the other. Noting historicist readers' tendencies to dismiss these elements in Schreiner's work, Lane argues for an essential tension between the erotic and the social, and for the inability of historicism to explain the traumas of desire and identification that shape this novel.

In what seemed to me the most thoughtful and original essay in this volume, Bradd Epps cautions against would-be queer readings of Juan Goytisolo that exalt the author's “subversive” — because (homo) sexually unapologetic — virtues. Invoking, in the name of the parodie and the “fragmentary,” what one admiring critic terms Goytisolo's “sodomyth” neglects the possibility that “by representing the sodomite as dangerous, deadly and destructive, as subversive, [the sodomyth] may serve to legitimate, yet again, an apparatus of control and punishment. Indeed, so mythified, subversion may itself actually shore up the dominant order” (205). Even if the fragmenting power of the “sodomyth” can be allowed, writes Epps, “fragmentation as a general concept, strategy, and value should be critically interrogated. Fragmentation can only be completely “positive,” politically, ethically, and aesthetically speaking, when it becomes coherent and unambiguous, when it ceases to be fragmentation” (207). Subversion and fragmentation, as one might infer from this, only make good on their promise of emancipation if they envision and guide us toward some new system, some other, albeit radically different whole. Last fall, just seven months after the incredible tragedy that left 15 members of their school community dead and 23 wounded, the Columbine High School Rebels won the Colorado state football championships for the first time. All of the players wore the number 70 on their helmets, in honor of their teammate Matt Kechter, who was one of the students killed in the April 20, 1999 tragedy. Matt himself should have worn the number 70 this fall in what would have been his senior year. The crowd chanted “We are Columbine” as the Rebels played the Bruins of Cherry Creek (“Columbine Wins”). It became a slogan of victory and reclamation.

Mike Sheehan, president of the Columbine High School student body in the year following the massacre, greeted a gathering of 2,700 students and parents on the first morning of school at a “Take Back our School Rally:” “Good morning, Columbine! It's so great to see so many of you out here today to take back our school.” He drew the crowd's attention to a sign restored over the entrance to the school that reads: “Through these halls pass the finest kids in America, the students of Columbine High School” (Olinger et al. 8A). At the same rally, principal Frank DeAngelis said, amidst cheers from the crowd, “I have waited for months to say this, and I say it with great pride: Columbine, we are back” (Janofsky 21).

Re-entry to the school in September was framed as reclamation: “We are Columbine” and “We are back.” What does that mean? What were they as a school and as a community prior to the tragic massacre on April 20? What are they now? “How could it happen here?” is a question often asked in communities like Columbine where school violence seems unthinkable. Clearly, many factors contributed to the crimes: some unique to Eric and Dylan and the Littleton community and others more broadly representative of boys and school communities.

In this paper, we will focus on the gender components that may have contributed to the crimes. There is an incontestable relationship between gender and school violence: school shootings are committed by boys. The perpetrators don't commit violence at school because they are boys. But what about their being boys contributes to their committing the violence? It is this question that we will attempt to answer in this paper. We will use feminist psychodynamic theory to address relational differences in boys and girls that may have played a role in this tragedy. Also, we will consider how males and females are socialized differently in our society, in their homes, and in their schools and their communities, and how this difference made Eric and Dylan, because they were boys, vulnerable to rage and violence. Further, because these boys didn't fit into the “myth” of masculinity, they may have been more likely than their peers to attempt to prove their manhood through active violence.

In Speaking with the Devil: Exploring Senseless Acts of Evil, Carl Goldberg takes the reader on a trip through regions of the human psyche that most of us try to avoid. Goldberg's central focus in this book is on malevolence, which he defines as “the deliberate infliction of cruel, painful suffering on another living being” (4). For me, it was easily the scariest trip I've ever been on, but not really because of the rogue's gallery of monstrous characters and devilish deeds that Goldberg has assembled for this reflective adventure. Without a doubt, the most powerfully threatening part of the trip was a moment near the end when I found myself staring directly into the face of evil and realized, much to my horror, that the face looking back at me was my own. My initial instinct at this point was exactly the same as it had been 30 years earlier at a similar point in my youth: I wanted to get very far away from my infernal visage as fast as I could. But, unlike my adolescent flight from haunting reflection, I was unable to cut and run on this occasion. Goldberg had me exactly where he wanted me and he wasn't about to let me run away this time. He had worked too hard in this book to create this valuable opportunity to help me learn about myself, and he would not let it go to waste. Instead, Goldberg wrapped the reassuring arms of his rational analysis around me and provided me the mature guidance I had needed during my adolescent flight from the devil within me. In the process, Goldberg taught me a number of very important lessons. He taught me that I have a personal responsibility to understand and control malevolence, not because I am a monstrous freak of nature but simply because I am an ordinary human being and, therefore, the seeds of malevolent behavior exist within me as they exist within all of us. He also taught me about my self-protective instincts to deny these facts and to distance myself from anyone I perceive as an agent of evil. Finally, he taught me to recognize that my best hope for controlling expressions of my own malevolence is by maintaining intimate personal connections with others and, most important, with myself.

This recent collection of essays provides a compelling and wide-ranging discussion of violence in the arts, provoked in certain terms, as editor Christopher Sharrett notes in his introduction, by the numerous school shootings at the time of its publication. These horrific shootings, writes Sharrett, seem to have arisen in a time “correlated with a devaluation of the human subject and the increased sense of no future that is the hallmark of late capitalist society” (11). The essays in this volume, therefore, circulate around representations of violence in this particular postmodern context. Published as a part of the Books in Contemporary Film and Television Series, the collection attends most closely to the violent visual image, whether it is rituals of bloodletting in current cinema, or the predatory camera work of tabloid television, or a series such as the wildly popular drama Cops. Essays range from such topics as The X-Files, the films of John Woo, iconographie serial killer Jeffrey Dahmer, and the martyred body of Mel Gibson, as well as discussions on such conspicuous ultra-violent films as Natural Born Killers (1994), Kalifornia (1993), and not-so-violent films such as Forrest Gump (1994). The volume consistently resists positing that these representations are direct causes of further violence in contemporary society, opting instead for a more complicated reading. All of the contributors in fact appear to operate from the premise that the violent image is, as Sharrett describes it, an “artifact embodying ideological assumptions” (10). Sharrett is careful to note in his introduction, for instance, that the word ‘mythologies’ in the book's title refers less to Jungian archetypal narratives expressing the self than to a series of ideological rituals promoted by systems of power. He sees the book arguing for “the importance of the violent image in furthering an atomized society that has been in the making since colonial forces took possession of this nation” (10).

Psychoanalytic cultural studies usually treat the nation as a collective projection of individual egos and as a mental extension of the maternal body. Scapegoating and ethnic hatred are interpreted as clinging to the symbiotic unity and repressing one's castration—i.e., the shift from the imaginary wholeness of primary narcissism into a separate being in the symbolic order represented by the father and adult sexuality. For instance, “greedy” Jews represented for the Nazis greedy siblings, who fulfilled their own dream to live parasitically off of the mother instead of working. Hate and envy, which the nationalists disown, are projected onto the others and the externalized feelings are polluting and poisoning the harmonious dual union between the nationalist/boy and nation/mother from the outside. The more the inner balance of a society is shattered, the more others as multifaceted beings will be homogenized and—at worst—deanimated in order to produce united groups bent under one will.1

Thus, these overly organic metaphors of “nation” in texts and imagery make psychoanalytically oriented researchers suspect either arrested individual development or displaced social conflict—or both at the same time.

Media researchers Carolyn Marvin and David W. Ingle, in their study on sacrificial wishes and rituals around the American flag, agree that the flag is revered in patriotic rituals as the embodiment of a bloodthirsty totem god who organizes killing energy. But they reject any psychoanalytic hermeneutics and claim that ever-recurrent blood sacrifices of young men, leaders, or outsiders indicate only irreversible ontology of social bonds, structural functions, rather than primitive remnants or developmental defects in identity formation.

According to their Durkheimean theory, the sacrifice renews the group's agreement to be a group. “The totem secret, the collective group taboo, is the knowledge that society depends on the death of its own members at the hands of the group” (2, 21). Marvin and Ingle disclose the totem secret only to acknowledge it as inevitable. Making the secret conscious does not alter the practice of creating group cohesion by turning volunteer insiders into outsiders and letting the “enemy” execute them so that the group could be rejuvenated by drinking their blood. Group sentiment flows from the value of the lifeblood shed by the community members. The social body is periodically renewed at the cost of individual bodies; the nation is always constituted in the last sacrifice that counts for the living. Thus the nation is literally created out of the flesh of its citizens, and the flag functions as an agent and sign of the nation formed in blood sacrifice.

Shortly after a series of violent episodes in schools culminating in the deaths of fifteen students at Columbine High School in Littleton, Colorado, it appeared that a change might take place in the longstanding inability of the U.S. government to control the distribution of firearms. Much was made in the press of the horrors of the massacre in Littleton and the need for a response. Many thought Congress would have no choice but to enact legislation to control the access to guns that turned hatred and the associated violent impulses into murder on a large scale. They were wrong.

No more than two months after the Littleton shootings, even the most inconsequential limitation on access to guns was meeting with intense resistance on Capital Hill. Under the headline “House Undertakes Days-Long Battle on Youth Violence,” The New York Times reported on June 17: “A bitterly divided House plunged today into the nation's culture wars, passionately debating long into the night whether school prayer, a clampdown on violence in entertainment, stiff prison sentences or gun control was the answer to the spate of school shootings that have left teen-agers dead.”

On one side were gun control advocates, mainly Democrats, who might not believe that guns kill people, but remain convinced that limiting access to guns would reduce the likelihood that people with guns would kill people. The other side had lately turned to matters of religion and culture, one Congressman insisting that the “entertainment industry gets away literally with murder…. Anyone that doesn't think rotten movies, rotten rap lyrics, rotten video games aren't poisoning—toxically poisoning—our kid's minds and making some kids think that's acceptable, just isn't paying attention.” The House minority whip formulated the problem in religious terms: “What message is sent when it is illegal to pray in schools? … This rejection of God must change.” Out of all this rancor, the House succeeded in passing a measure allocating $1.5 billion to be distributed to state and local government “for aggressive prosecution, punishment, and prevention of juvenile crime.” The next day, a measure was passed to allow the posting of the Ten Commandments in schools. If the problem is youth violence, then prayer in school, support for “family values,” and aggressive punishment is the solution.

The “Cause” of Sex; or, the Discontent of Liberal Theory

Susan Varney

Susan Varney

Susan Varney   Graduate student in literature at SUNY Buffalo, where she is completing a dissertation tentatively entitled, “Virtue in Chains: Liberty, Equality, Sexual Difference.” She has published articles on British modern literature as well as feminist and psychoanalytic theory.

If there is one discontent that can be said to have helped shape intellectual thought in this century, it is a general discontent with the liberal tradition as it has thus far developed: a fear that it is somehow responsible for enabling such political perversions as fascism and totalitarianism, that it is insufficiently responsive to questions of social welfare and overly dependent upon a sometimes brutal system of retributive justice. The discontent of which I shall speak, however, is the one that has plagued liberal theory from the outset: its incapacity to recognize the political relevance of sexual difference. From almost its inception, liberal theory has been plagued by a feminist critique that charges it with failing to recognize the sexual inequality inherent in its own conception of universal rights. As has been repeatedly noted, liberal theory gave women the grounds upon which to demand rights for themselves, to ask that this “universalist” conception of rights apply to them as well. On the other hand, by asserting that women deserved access to these rights as much as men, feminists contested the very logic upon which this system of “universal rights” had been conceived—namely, the concept of the “abstract individual.” By asking for rights on behalf of women, feminists unavoidably made sex a political issue. Suddenly the question of rights was also a question of sex and, whether a feminist adopted a position of equality or difference, the fact remained that she was making an argument for the relevance of sexuality in a discourse that had declared such issues of subjective particularity to be outside its domain. Feminism thus put sex on the political table and, in so doing, introduced the problem of particularity into a political discourse seemingly founded on its potential eradicability. In what follows I don't necessarily want to dispute Lacan's thesis that it was Marx who was the first to invent the symptom. However, I do want to note a) that it was liberal theory that produced the symptom Marx was arguably the first to theorize, and b) that it was the feminist discontent to which liberalism gave rise that first pointed in that critical direction when it insisted on the political relevance of the question of sexual difference.

Introduction

Women have served all these centuries as looking-glasses possessing the magic and delicious power of reflecting the figure man at twice its natural size.

Virginia Woolf, A Room of One's Own

In an interview published in Hypatia, Luce Irigaray insists, perhaps to the outrage of many traditional philosophers, that she too is a philosopher (Hirsh and Olson 97).1 Despite her multiple identities—a feminist, a psychoanalyst, and a linguist—Irigaray defines herself solely as a philosopher. This deliberate move2 works to subvert traditional philosophy, which she argues depends upon the repression of women. In a similar critical vein, Michèle Le Doeuff, another French feminist philosopher, in her famous essay “Women and Philosophy,” poses the following rhetorical question:

But what are they worried about? Where is the threat to philosophy in women being capable of it? It might be suggested that the so-called sovereignty of philosophy is at stake here…. When a respected activity admits women it loses its value. … It may be the great dignity of philosophy that keeps women away from it; conversely for this great dignity to be maintained, women must be kept away. (191)

Only through denying that women are capable of stating or judging the credibility of philosophical statements does philosophy earn its status as the “queen of the sciences,” Le Doeuff suggests here. Exclusions operate to exalt one group to a renowned status, while leaving the masses behind. If just anyone was capable of philosophical insight, then philosophical insights would be mediocre utterances proffered by the hoi polloi. Not everyone is able to discern abstract and universal truths, and so we must leave this to those who can—that is, we must leave this, as Hegel says, to men. “The man's dominion,” writes Hegel,

is scientific universal cognition,… [the] universal, a universal idea, the imagination inspired by reason, the Idea of a universal. These are the man's provinces. There can be exceptions for individual women, but the exception is not the rule. Women, when they trespass into these provinces, put the provinces themselves in danger. (525-526)

Judith Gurewich

Judith Gurewich

Judith Gurewich   Director of the Lacan Seminar at the Center for Literary and Cultural Studies at Harvard University. The title of the conference Oedipus Today seemed to make the assumption that the existence of the oedipal complex is the effect of a family structure dominated by a paternal figure whose function is to impose on his children the very law that makes society possible. If this assumption is correct, how do we comprehend the fact that an American conference on culture and psychoanalysis chooses to implicitly dismiss over fifty years of psychoanalytic research, research that has kept psychoanalysis alive precisely by chipping away at the oedipal dynamics and their vicissitudes: from object relations, to self psychology, most post-Freudian theories have successfully undermined the paternal function. They brought to the forefront of the psychoanalytic stage the very psychic connection that resists the pull of social change: the pre-oedipal dynamics and the nurturing function of the mother.

For most of American psychoanalysis, therefore, the question of Oedipus Today was resolved long ago. Yet for the organizers of this conference, who clearly have not been sitting on the margins of history, the issue is still burning.

If this assumption is correct, the title Oedipus Today recognizes that the post-Freudian approaches are based on premises that no longer fit the prerequisites of the present academic debate. This debate is informed by the epistemological cut that structuralism imposed on the human sciences in general, and on psychoanalysis in particular. By placing the emphasis on the preoedipal, post-Freudian theories have sidestepped the most tricky part of the oedipal story—namely, its impact on sexual difference and gender roles. Moreover, by rejecting what they perceive to be Freud's biological determinism, the post-Freudian have returned to a pre-Freudian, even pre-Durkheimean, position. Having thrown out the Oedipus complex, they have ended up with a concept of an individual who, while interacting with the social, is nevertheless not produced by it.

This being said, the problematic status of the Oedipus complex remains intact. If Lacan's psychoanalytic vision of a subject who is both produced and divided by language has gotten fairly good ratings in certain academic circles, this is not to say that Lacan has explicitly resolved the aporia that plagues Freud's discovery of the unconscious: if the Oedipus complex is a universal phenomenon that accounts for the psychic mapping of human subjectivity, how can we subtract from such a proposition the historical circumstances that made such a discovery possible? Can we distinguish, in the manifest content of nineteenth-century Vienna, a latent structure that can be refound in any place at any time?

A white male student responds to a rigorous critique of US history by a black male social theorist with a pantomimed response to what he and other students believe is the emotional subtext of the book. He stands, drops the book on the floor, kicks it across the room, stoops—ostensibly to retrieve it—and kicks it again as fellow students laugh and applaud with approval.

Gay and lesbian students respond to a memoir of disappointed lesbian love with smirks. They explain to the instructor that they are unable to identify with what they take as obsessive devotion—that passion of this sort is both “unhealthy” and unnecessary in an age when romantic partners can be replaced with ease.2

Students in a public policy class watch a PBS documentary that focuses on federal welfare reform legislation and its effects on poor women and children. In discussion immediately following the viewing, they criticize the irrational affect of the women interviewed in the film.3 Further discussion clarifies that they have forgotten—or failed to hear—all crucial pieces of information in the film that situate the women's speech and affect.

Among the issues addressed by feminist pedagogy are the ways in which the discourses of subordinated groups are incorporated into mainstream educational contexts. In this essay I take up one dimension of this issue: the experience of teaching undergraduate students using identity-group texts that adopt or express a passionate style of discourse. What I shall call passionate pedagogy is often viewed with suspicion and resisted, or disavowed, especially—but not only—by students whose social identities are dominant in terms of race, gender, or sexuality.4 I shall argue that the resistance toward and disavowal of passionate pedagogy by undergraduate students can be illuminated by examining political and psychological dimensions of the split between public and private political spheres that helps to structure the realms of politics, subjectivity, and discourse in our society, and especially students' processes of constituting themselves in ways that are consistent with this split. The resources for such a political and psychological analysis are available within feminist theory, although they are too frequently dispersed under different perspectives within feminism.

Revolutionary Neurotics and the Cunning of Conservatism

Mary Caputi

Mary Caputi

Mary Caputi   Associate Professor of political theory at California State University, Long Beach. Her areas of interest include feminist thought, critical theory, and psychoanalysis. She is the author of Voluptuous Yearnings: A Feminist Theory of the Obscene.

Introduction

In its attention to internal conflict and disavowed ambivalences, psychoanalytic theory often makes trouble for the instigators of social change. This theory unveils a conservative drift lodged within even the most maverick impulse, highlighting the ambivalence of political conviction and subsequent difficulty of bringing about social change. The revolutionary's identity is indeed overdetermined in nature, and certain tenets of psychoanalytic thought help explain the conservative identifications that sometimes lie hidden behind subversive action. At times, then, a society's progressive forces ironically gravitate toward those institutionalized forms of power and authority they publicly oppose, replaying what they seek to dismantle and unwittingly repackaging what they hope to destroy. In this essay, I analyze why even the most revolutionary elements of a culture can ultimately display mimetic, conservative tendencies. I do this by focusing on those trends which identify strongly with the very framework they oppose and thus reproduce that framework in sometimes deliberate, sometimes subconscious ways. My specific interest lies with the deep ambivalences and neurotic orientation of the colonial setting as described by Frantz Fanon.

Psychoanalytic theory offers at least two reasons why social change is often stymied by its own instigators, whose ambivalent, doubled sense of self confounds their good intentions. One reason pertains to the melancholia to which we are all susceptible, a sadness that confirms our resistance to change and consequent love of the status quo. Authors such as Julia Kristeva and Judith Butler build on Freud's basic theory to argue that melancholia is central in allowing subjectivity to emerge at all; integral to gender formation, it exists as an experience at the very bedrock of our social identities. Despite our familiarity with this tenebrous state, however, we never grow accustomed to its distressing influence. For given its ability to pulverize and to dishearten, melancholia makes us all suspicious of change, clinging to what we know and eager for continuity.

James Penney PHD

James Penney

James Penney   Candidate in the Literature Program at Duke University, where he is currently completing a dissertation entitled “The World of Perversion: Psychoanalysis and the Impossible Absolute of Desire.” He recently contributed an essay on Julia Kristeva to The Psychoanalysis of Race.

In this, his most recent book, Slavoj Žižek continues the two-pronged project he inaugurated a decade ago with his path-breaking The Sublime Object of Ideology: to deepen, first, the project upon which Lacan himself first embarked in his seminars of re-interpreting the history of philosophy from the perspective of psychoanalytic conceptuality; and to develop, second, a political engagement with contemporary culture through the lens of Lacanian theory. Readers new to Žižek's work will be delighted to discover one of current theory's most brilliant minds at the peak of his form whose occasional philosophical density is counterbalanced by a talent for illustrating nuanced concepts through entertaining references to popular culture. Seasoned veterans of Žižek-reading, for their part, will encounter what amounts to the author's most politically consequential work to date, in which the ramifications of Lacanian theory for political praxis are spelled out in an unprecedented manner through analyses of the work of numerous authors who heretofore have been either treated cursorily or altogether absent from Žižek's work. The scope of this ambitious book is extraordinarily broad; we will attempt in consequence to provide a concise overview of its fundamental conceptual moves, and then focus on two of Žižek's interventions: his rearticulation of leftist political agency through Lacanian ethics and his extended engagement with Anglo-American queer theory through a dialogue with Judith Butler.

Though it does not feature an extensive dialogue with Descartes, The Ticklish Subject begins with a characteristically polemical and deliberately provocative statement: that the aporetic discourses of contemporary theory—from postmodern deconstructionism to critical post-Marxism, from New Age obscurantism to the post-epistemology of cognitive science—share an obfuscatory inaugural theoretical gesture—namely, the rejection of the allegedly Cartesian, self-transparent thinking subject of modernity. Žižek, in contrast, seeks to rehabilitate this subject, not as it has been falsely characterized in the preceding discourses, but as it is mobilized by Lacan, who claimed that Descartes was the first to formulate a psychoanalytic theory of subjectivity. For Žižek, the Cartesian cogito is not the reassuring subject of knowledge whose grasp of a rational universe is grounded by God, but rather a subject split between thought and being: a subject who may only grasp his existence by apprehending an alien, external cognitive agency that thinks on his behalf (“I am, therefore it thinks” thus becomes the correct axiom of the Cartesian subjectivity).

Adolescent Satanism: An Intersubjective and Cultural Perspective

Timothy Zeddies

Timothy Zeddies

Timothy Zeddies   The University of Texas Health Science Center—San Antonio. He is on the editorial board of Psychoanalytic Psychology, is outgoing Co-Chair of the Graduate Student Committee for the Division of Psychoanalysis (39) of the American Psychological Association, and is Chair of the Film Studies Group and a member of the Education and Training Committee of the San Antonio Society for Psychoanalytic Studies.

Ever since Freud's disparaging comments on religion and spirituality, psychoanalysis has tended not to deal with how their various expressions—including mysticism, Satanism, and the occult—impact treatment. The general tendency to minimize or marginalize the impact of the occult notwithstanding, analytic practitioners who work in psychiatric in-patient or residential settings know all too well how appealing Satanism and cultism are to adolescent patients. Aside from a few exceptions (e.g., Olsson; Cushman; Chasseguet-Smirgel), however, there is almost nothing in the psychoanalytic literature on the topic. In my experience in treating adolescents involved in Satanism, a deeper appreciation of their interest and participation in satanic activities, readings, and dress is often a vital aspect of successful treatment. It therefore behooves us to develop a better understanding of how Satanism can impact the lives of adolescents.

In this article, I attempt to bring together two worlds that are relatively unknown to each other: psychoanalysis and adolescent Satanism. I briefly review the empirical literature on the topic, as well as a few key ideas from intersubjectivity theory, which I suggest offers a clinical perspective that can enrich and deepen our understanding of adolescent Satanism. In the final section, I offer some thoughts on how adolescent Satanism acts as a foil to some of the deepest and most precious values and beliefs of Western culture with which, in many respects, we may be in danger of losing touch.

Literature Review

Empirical Literature

Over the last 10 or 15 years, there has been a dramatic increase in youth involvement in cults, including Satanism, street gangs, and skinhead groups. Harrowing examples of the destruction and violence these cults create have been graphically illustrated in the last couple years. Several incidents of school violence and mass murder—including Columbine High School in Colorado in 1999, Thurston High School in Oregon in 1998, and Pearl High School in Mississippi in 1997—have gripped the entire country, leaving us baffled, horrified, and desperate for answers.1 In spite of this, there is a relative paucity of literature on the subject, particularly adolescent Satanism. As a result, this phenomenon and its influence on the actions and beliefs of today's youth remain poorly understood by a majority of mental health practitioners, and a source of fear and trepidation for many parents and educators.

This paper indicates a lacuna in social science explanation: that rising rates of exclusion from schools, which is a significant social issue, has received little attention from social scientists and has largely remained unexplained. Our suggestion is that this lacuna can be filled if we understand the psychodynamics of exclusion in general and of exclusion from schools in particular. Robert Samuels

Robert Samuels

Robert Samuels   Received his Doctorate in Psychoanalysis from the University of Paris VIII. He is currently teaching writing at the University of California at Santa Barbara. He is the author of Between Philosophy and Psychoanalysis: Lacans Reconstruction of Freud and Hitchcock's Bi-Textuality: Lacan, Feminisms, and Queer Theory. In response to the shootings at the Columbine High School, various media outlets and politicians blamed everyone and everything from school teachers, parents, video games, and web sites, to teenage depression, prejudice, media depictions of violence, and peer-group bullying. I will argue that if we develop a psychoanalytic conception of postmodern culture, we can connect all of these separate causes in order to understand the function of violence in today's society. Moreover, this understanding of postmodern culture can help us to propose a more effective educational response to the contemporary problem of teenage violence. For even though people want to believe that every social problem has a single cause or answer, it is the combination of many diverse factors that often contributes to the complicated nature of these conflicts, and a unifying concept like postmodern culture can help us to bring together these disparate factors.

On the most basic level, postmodern culture embodies four main attributes: (1) the increase capitalistic production and distribution of information (mass media, internet, universal education); (2) a blending of fact and fiction (virtual reality, science fiction, spectacle culture); (3) a subjective sense of helplessness and passivity; and (4) a lost sense of authority, originality, and shared values. All of these aspects of our current society can be related to the different causes of teenage violence and the Columbine incident. While violence has always existed in human history, I will argue that the structure of postmodern culture changes the nature and effects of aggression and hatred within society. For what we find in the Columbine High School example is in many ways an exaggeration of central aspects of our current media culture of violence. In order to develop a psychoanalytic criticism of this new mode of violence, I will first discuss the Columbine tragedy and then relate it to an analysis of professional wrestling. I will conclude by outlining a program of action to combat some of the most destructive aspects of our postmodern culture.

What prompts adolescent boys to murder, terrorize, and commit suicide within the confines of their school building? How can they perpetuate these crimes against their peers? What is their motivation for violence against those individuals who make up their adolescent community? These are the questions that find us grappling with the dissonance of confusion, misunderstanding, and denial. The most common wish among parents and professionals is to believe that there is some pathological reason for the actions of an adolescent perpetrator. This wish empowers us to study the psychology of the individual. What went wrong with the adolescent? Could it be psychosis, drugs, lack of parental involvement, or access to guns? Delving into the individual psychology saves us from asking scarier questions with less tangible answers. However, the events perpetrated by adolescents in recent years implore us to investigate more closely the myriad issues beyond the scope of the individual. By committing violent acts against peers and themselves in their school buildings, teenagers such as Dylan Klebold and Eric Harris of Littleton, Colorado demonstrate the need for an investigation into the impact of group dynamics within adolescent communities.

In this paper, we will present selected key concepts from the psychoanalytic literature on groups and apply them to the school shootings at Columbine High School in Littleton, Colorado.1 More specifically, we will describe how the group's unconscious processes led to the development of particular roles for Dylan Kleboid and Eric Harris. We will use psychoanalytic concepts such as projective identification, the defense mechanism of splitting, basic assumptions groups, and the social defense system to develop the position that Dylan Klebold and Eric Harris were the recipients of the group's projections and, further, that the group was complicit in developing their role as offenders. At the same time, we will consider the impact of groups in the particular developmental stage of adolescence. Finally, we will discuss the implications for school psychologists, teachers, administrators, and other mental health professionals in schools.

The theory and practice of psychoanalysis, like every human endeavor, is embedded in politics. From its early days in Victorian Vienna to its current diversified manifestations, psychoanalysis has challenged political ideologies with its implicit radicalism. The attribution of unconscious motivation to human behavior, the lifting of repression, and the liberation of sexuality are just as much psychological statements as they are political. These statements reflect the subversive if not revolutionary subtext of Freudian thinking. Psychoanalysis aims at liberating the psyche from its oppressors and persecutors. To be a psychoanalyst is to be a critic of the social order, its value, and its demands for conformity. Psychic conflicts may be understood as pathological configurations which grow out of the struggle between the pull to conform to social demands and the wish to rebel against them.

Although numerous presentations and publications have unveiled the dilemma confronted by analysts in Europe before and after World War II, little attention has been paid to the fate of Argentine or South African analysts during and after suffering the most oppressive dictatorship of the second half of the twentieth century.1

Unlike Argentina, where the development of psychoanalysis mirrored the vicissitudes of the discipline in Europe (particularly England and France), and where its place on the cultural map was firmly established for decades prior to the military dictatorship,2 in Apartheid South Africa psychoanalysis was characterized by the paucity of its contributions and its limited and restricted applications. The latter is not surprising since South Africa was the land of silence for centuries, and therefore all social disciplines, if allowed to develop, did so at the service of Apartheid. Psychoanalysis became a forbidden fruit which could only be purchased in foreign lands. England and America became the training grounds for those mental health practitioners who wanted to train as psychoanalysts. However, most South African psychoanalysts never went back to South Africa, building new homes in exile. It was not until 1998, on the occasion of the first psychoanalytic conference, entitled “Change: Psychoanalytic Perspectives,” held in Capetown, that South African analysts returned. The conference was organized by a group of South African expatriate psychoanalysts (the South African Psychoanalysis Trust) and sponsored by the International Psychoanalytic Association. The overall aim of the conference was to establish a dialogue about the potential role psychoanalysis might play in post-Apartheid South Africa.
