Since the beginning of the year, the Detroit area has been gifted with offerings in developmental psychoanalysis that seem to put the recent grotesque expressions of aggression in young people in some perspective. The Michigan Psychoanalytic Council held a conference on Violence and Aggression in Children on February 20, 2000 in Ann Arbor. Jack and Kerry Kelly Novick, psychoanalysts well known for their published work in the area of sadomasochism and for their foundation of an analytically informed preschool in Allen Creek, Michigan (Ann Arbor), opened the conference with “The Early Childhood Roots of Aggression and Violence.” Both Jack and Kerry were trained at the Anna Freud Center and are supervising analysts with the Michigan Psychoanalytic Institute. Jack is also a supervising analyst with the New York Freudian Society.

Based on the truism that a picture is worth a thousand words, their paper actually provided captioning for a remarkable video presentation. Mildly reminiscent of the 16 mm. Rene Spitz 1940s “hospitalism”/ anaclitically depressed orphan and the “refrigerator mother” movies of undergraduate days, the video demonstrated the making of a psychopath in a very dynamic and chillingly subtle way. The camera was focused on a mother-infant pair, living in a home for unwed mothers, who engaged with each other in a gradually more disturbing way.

The mother, who had emerged from a profoundly abusive background, could not help but allow her noxious objects to infest the relationship with sadistically interruptive behaviors. She dislodged her baby from his play scheme, displaced his attention, and constantly shifted and offset the sense of relatedness both to her and to the (potentially transitional) objects within the small world around them. Her thoughtless behavior seemed obligatory as she whispered increasingly degrading and malicious remarks to her infant-toddler son in a sweet and seductive way while fostering an unsettled disquietude within the play space. The regularity and smoothness of the play work were punctuated by repeated fracturing as mother interacted in a provocatively disjointed manner, now offering him an object of play, now artfully and dispassionately throwing another into the path of his awareness just as he begins to invest his small and burgeoning self in the original item's exquisite facets of design and meaning-making.

“He was their son—but they didn't know the kid who did this.”

(The minister who buried Dylan Klebold; qtd. in Goodman)

Introduction: The Concentric Circles of a School Shooting1

I set for myself three inter-related tasks in this essay: (1) an understanding of the massacre at Columbine High School in Littleton, Colorado, on April 20, 1999; (2) an understanding of physical violence (with knives, guns, bombs) perpetrated by adolescents in America; and (3) an understanding of the psychodynamics of American culture, of which (1) and (2) are at once symptom and metaphor. I shall argue that the slaughter of youth by youth at that Colorado school is in part an extension of the rage against the imminent disposability felt by tens of millions of Americans in an increasingly corporate-dominated culture. In the process, I hope to illumine such behavioral science conundrums as understanding human aggression, understanding contemporary “violence in the workplace” (a widespread social problem and category; see Allcorn, Anger), and understanding the relationship among perpetrators, victims, and bystanders (Hilberg)—a relationship that constitutes a single overarching culture.

This paper will explore the very nature of psychodynamically informed cultural explanation for a catastrophe that has been exposed to universal gaze and interpretation by satellite-facilitated television. Specifically, how does one conceptually link large cultural processes (indeed, species-specific human biology) with local events? Specifically, how do social processes, structures, values, and change in the wider culture contribute to the triggering and later construction of such events as the Littleton, Colorado, high school massacre? Further, how do cultures explain “themselves” to “themselves”?

In summary, this study will attempt to bridge the exploration of a single catastrophic event with the larger epistemological issue of psychodynamically informed cultural explanation itself. Stated differently, it will address the interlinked questions of: What kind of people does this? What kind of culture does this happen in? And What kind of animal (in the phylogenetic sense) does this? My working metaphor to organize this paper is a kind of mental map, in which one proceeds outwardly from the center of a circle—the shooting itself—to progressively further, more encompassing circles of understanding and explanation (an image I owe to Mark Bracher, personal communication, January 11, 2000).

In this paper I will argue that a psychoanalytic approach to sociological interview methodology necessarily involves a process of listening to, learning from, and interpreting experience. Within the context of this process I will address one of the central concerns of sociological research, the idea of interviewer “matching”: that we should use black researchers to interview black respondents, and women to interview women. I will highlight what I believe to be serious concerns about this premise and set them within the context of a research project that I have undertaken into the experience of black and Asian students in a British higher education institute.

I have previously outlined how I think a psychoanalytic approach to fieldwork can benefit sociological analysis. Hunt suggests that subjectivity and self understanding are critical to well executed fieldwork. A psychoanalytic perspective offers us an understanding of how sociological data is both structured and constructed. There are two main areas in which psychoanalytic fieldwork differs from conventional sociological method. First there is the notion that the unconscious plays a role in the construction of our reality and the way in which we perceive others. Second, the unconscious plays a significant part in both the generation of research data and the construction of the research environment. Thus we have a number of areas where unconscious forces affect research: the choice of research subject and setting, as Hunt notes, may reflect an “inner dynamic.” For example, a deep interest in racism may reflect certain incidents or events in a researcher's past that become disguised as curiosity or professional interest. Once the research is under way, unconscious forces mediate encounters between researcher and researched. The interview is an arena of conscious and unconscious interplay between researcher and respondent (see Sherwood).

The Interview: Listening to and Learning from Experience

In a recent research project I interviewed a number of black and Asian students to try and understand their experience of higher education at a British university. All the students were volunteers and undergraduates in the same institution. (It is not my intention in this paper to discuss the results of the project but to reflect on the research methodology. I am not a psychoanalytic practitioner but a sociologist whose epistemological outlook is influenced by psychoanalysis. The whole interview process was therefore a case of learning from experience for me, both in terms of listening to the respondent and reflecting on the dynamic between researcher and researched.)

Psychoanalysis takes two, one to speak and one to listen. A distance between sender and receiver is necessary if together they are to identify a latent meaning in the discourse. One could thus object to Jay Prosser's text that he seems to produce the discourse of trans-sexuality without attention to a latent meaning. He speaks very eloquently, but he is not listening.

Since transsexuals do not usually address their demand to the psychoanalyst but rather to the surgeon, it is permissible to conclude that a listening with the third ear is not what is expected. The writer of a theoretical work is however in a different category altogether, since the book must encounter readers in order to exist, and if the work is to make a scientific contribution, its message must not limit itself to a capture on the level of the imaginary.

Prosser proposes to treat “body and narrative—in their relation to transsexuality”: “My primary purpose in reading transsexual narratives is to introduce into cultural theory a trajectory that foregrounds the bodily matter of gender crossings” (4).

For a transsexual to achieve the acting out of sex change, the demand for hormones and surgery has not historically been enough; a narrative has had to be produced, a story which would result in the clinician pronouncing the diagnosis which would permit treatment. More than twenty years ago, Robert Stoller recognized that the biographies produced upon the demand of the medical establishment by candidates for sex change operations had little value for psychoanalysis, since they feature memories organized in function of the demand for transformation. He recommended not taking them at face value, or rather adopting an attitude of prudence and attention to precise clinical details. This is to say that he did not wish to accept this discourse without analysis. What risks going unperceived in these autobiographies that are organized in terms of a manifest demand is the message of the unconscious.

As Prosser notes, in the context of a sex change program, the candidate's capacity to narrativize the embodiment of his/her condition, to tell a coherent story of transsexual experience, is required by the doctors before, as a condition of, their authorization of the subject's transformation. The story documents a history of gender identity which the medical intervention would only render visible to others.

Introduction

The publication of Robert Cormier's The Chocolate War in 1974 marks one of those watershed moments when the terms of how we understand adolescent literature and culture are profoundly changed. A boy refuses to participate in his school's chocolate sale. He is threatened, tortured, and eventually publicly beaten and (presumably) killed for his nonconformity.1 Through this text, the reader is forced to confront the horrors of contemporary teen culture—its mandates, its cruelties, its relentless assault on the individual. Also through this text, the reader is introduced to a new kind of figure in adolescent literature and culture—the abject hero.

The shootings at Columbine High School in 1999 mark another such watershed. Two boys, operating at the social rim of their environment, targeted people whom they perceived as being “plugged in” to some group or some identity, be it Christian, athlete, popular crowd, etc. These are precisely the kinds of connections that elude the abject person; as an outsider, he or she has an intensely ambivalent relationship toward the walls that prevent him or her from fitting in. The tension between despising people for whom such connections work and being desirous yet unable to forge those connections themselves erupts in violent and aggressive acts toward the others who make it look so easy. The media is quick to call the perpetrators “monsters,” and to configure such outbreaks of teenage violence as isolated events even as they paradoxically map their occurrence all over the country. The effect of this kind of media attention serves to further isolate people who have already constructed themselves as outsiders, people who cannot seem to fit in with any particular crowd. These teens are living out the condition of abjection. Adolescent fiction that deals with abjection offers us both a means of understanding abjection and its contribution to violent behavior as well as some possible strategies for dealing with abjection that might reduce violence.

This paper is about listening. It sounds simple. In music and psychoanalysis, listening is something so fundamental as to be nearly taken for granted. Indeed, it might be easy to suppose there is little to be said that has not already been heard. There is an appreciable body of literature on psychoanalytic listening and, as for music, it goes without saying that listening is an absolute requisite. But the shared necessity of engaged listening is only the beginning.

I believe music2 and psychoanalysis most significantly overlap in the domain of emotion—the communication and registering of feelings. The aesthetic, philosophical, and psychological components underlying all manner of emotional response are intimately interrelated and, I contend, are substantively the same in music and the analytic situation; they are actually, not analogously, comparable.

There is also an historical connection.

It is humbling to recognize that the people I am supposed to be criticizing know more about the topic they are writing about than I do. It is disturbing to realize that I lack the integrative powers to give each paper its due, bringing them together to show how they elaborate a subtle theme none of us knew was there before I found it. That subtle theme is surely there, but I have not yet been able to find it. Instead, I will restrict myself to a not so subtle difference between two papers, begging Burack and Glass to accept my apologies that I have not been able to do justice to their fine papers.

If Caputi is right, then Wolfenstein is wrong. Wolfenstein writes that Du Bois is ambivalent about revolt and revenge, and that his ambivalence bears the mark of Oedipal guilt. To argue this, Wolfenstein has to resort to some pretty heavy-handed Freudian interpretation, such as interpreting the closing of John Jones' school as symbolic castration. The result is that Du Bois, or at least his characters such as John (not the same thing, it should be noted: sometimes authors use characters to represent positions they do not hold, or would be rid of), decline rebellion on moral as well as practical grounds. This, says Wolfenstein, is not good.

I like rage as well as the next person, but I wonder if Wolfenstein isn't seeing as castration what might better be seen as an acceptance of reality, above all the reality of racism, but also the reality of limits, mortality, and the very constrained goodness of the human species. Why can't Du Bois (or John; sometimes I'm not sure who Wolfenstein is writing about) be as melancholy as the rest of us—that is, all who think deeply about human life on this planet?

In this world there are but two ethical choices, and a thousand variations: to identify with the victim, or with the aggressor. As Caputi suggests, melancholy, maturity, the depressive position as Melanie Klein calls it, are all associated with identification with the victim. We are all victims of circumstances, some more than others of course, John more than most. To try to escape this melancholy via righteous rage may not be as invigorating and integrating as Wolfenstein seems to believe.

With the concern about school shootings and gangs, there has been much written and said recently about violence in adolescence. The prime question, of course, has been what causes it. In my view, there has been, unfortunately, far too much attention paid to the effects of films, video games, and other media influences on adolescent behavior. As a corollary to this, strong moral education has been seen as the source of good behavior. Just teach kids what's right firmly enough, and that will make them good. It repeatedly comes as a surprise to many that adolescents from good homes with good parents could become mass murderers. A psychoanalytic approach to understanding violence in adolescence can be helpful in understanding often neglected intrapsychic sources of violence in adolescence.

What special perspectives can a psychoanalytic view bring to the problem? There are several. First, as an approach that emphasizes the study of the individual case, a psychoanalytic view avoids a pitfall of other approaches: the fallacy that a particular behavior, in this case violence, has one source, the same source, in all violent people. This assumption of a single underlying source of an overt problem is a fallacy I have seen in the study of several areas of psychopathology. It sounds simple, but let me emphasize this point: there are many intrapsychic stories that may result in violent activity.

What are other unique perspectives that a psychoanalytic approach can bring to this problem? The role of the unconscious is one. The role of fantasy, both unconscious and conscious, is another. The psychology of conflict and the psychology of self-image are also central. The role of childhood, and especially early childhood, psychoanalysis considers basic to later development. Some more recent advances in the theory of affects are also very helpful in our effort. This all goes beyond simplistic efforts to search for external factors, often immediate or current ones, as the cause for violence in all violent teenagers.

In Who's That Girl? Who's That Boy? Clinical Practice Meets Postmodern Gender Theory, I put forth a theory of gender identity that drew both on work by relational analytic feminists, such as Benjamin, Dimen, Harris, and Goldner as well as work by poststructuralist feminists, such as Butler. I argued that the hallmark of all of this work is the premise that dominant categories of gender, race, sexuality, and class are derived from processes of splitting that are mandated by culturally sanctioned sexism, racism, heterosexism, and classism. For example, poststructuralists maintain that the category masculinity is in no way the mutually exclusive opposite of femininity; rather, masculinity exists as a category only by defining itself as what is not feminine. The two categories are meaningless except in relation to one another. Further, the relation between the categories is hierarchical, a differential power relation. The defining characteristics of masculinity have cultural value; what masculinity repudiates has less value.

As many cultural theorists have argued in the past ten or fifteen years (see, for example, Higginbotham; Connell), masculinity and femininity do not exist in isolation from other identity elements: black working-class heterosexual femininity, black middle-class heterosexual femininity, and black working or middle-class homosexual femininity are likely to be four different ways of experiencing gender. Thus, when speaking of dominant social categories, cultural theorists have taught us that it is more accurate to say that it is upper-class white heterosexual masculinity—rather than just masculinity—that holds the most clout. Indeed, the former is defined by repudiating all the other possible combinations of masculinity and femininity. On the cultural level, it is this repudiation that marks these categories as products of splitting. When we begin to look at all this on the level of psychic reality, on the level of how these categories are lived, we find the kind of splitting with which clinicians are most familiar. Let me give an example of how dominant white heterosexual masculinity might be constituted psychically: a white upper-middle-class male patient of mine, who struggles with not feeling masculine enough, reports one day his sense that the men in his firm who get rewarded are the macho pigs with no conscience. This observation fits firmly within his interpretation of his family history, in which, in several generations, some sons have been picked by parents to be feminized nice guys and some are molded to be ambitious sharks. He has disidentified with the sharks, but since that is his only template for masculinity, he feels feminine and lesser. He frequently complains about the men in his firm who get more attention from management than he, and one day he tells me a story about one such favorite. This man apparently proudly related to his secretary that when his 4-year old son called him on the phone, sobbing inconsolable he yelled at him to pull down his pants. Then he asked him what was between his legs. “A penis,” the son sobs. “Right,” dad replies. “So stop crying.” This simple lesson in masculinity well demonstrates poststructuralist arguments. This boy learns that to be a boy means not to be a girl. To be a boy means not to cry when something goes wrong; that's what girls do. To be a boy is to hide your vulnerability, to be stoic. He is taught, then, that culturally sanctioned masculinity is invulnerable, stoic. Masculine vulnerability will be culturally invisible to this boy and others like him—he might only recognize as masculine such images of dominant masculinity as the Marlboro Man or the heroes of action films. These cultural images appear to be seamlessly macho (despite revelations that the Marlboro Man was gay!). But how do things operate on the psychic level?

The Souls of Black Folk, first published in 1903, famously begins with the claim that “the problem of the Twentieth Century is the problem of the color-line” (5; hereafter Souls). The text is a multifaceted delineation of this problem and an equally multifaceted attempt to articulate a solution. In the latter regard and politically speaking, Du Bois marks out a middle path between accommodation and rebellion. Rejecting either “an attempt to adjust all thought and action to the will of the greater group” or “a feeling of revolt and revenge,” he argues for “a determined effort at self-realization and self-development despite environing opinion” (37). Despite environing opinion, and against it: “By every civilized and peaceful method we must strive for the rights which the world accords to men, clinging unwaveringly to those great words which the sons of the Fathers would fain forget: ‘We hold these truths to be self-evident: That all men are created equal; that they are endowed by their Creator with certain inalienable rights; that among these are life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness’” (45).

Du Bois's approach to solving the problem of the color-line centers the cultural explorations of Souls; and—with no little assistance from Du Bois himself—it centered the struggle for black liberation throughout the better part of the twentieth century. It is open to alternative interpretations and strategic adjustments; indeed, Du Bois construed it varyingly over time. Leaving aside the variances, however, one might make the argument that it dialectically resolves the opposition between the rejected alternatives of accommodation and revolt, preserving what is workable in each while leaving behind the self-defeating aspects. But unlike in the ideal world of Hegelian dialectics, in the real world all such syntheses are imperfect and incomplete. Residues of unresolved problems trail after them and the roads not taken continue to beckon. In the present instance, the pathway of accommodation may be safely disregarded. Du Bois was unambivalent in his rejection of it and it plays only a rearguard role historically.1 Not so the “feeling of revolt and revenge,” which he refused to embrace but could not entirely suppress.

“All animals are equal, but some are more equal than others are.” This quote from Orwell could very well function as an epitaph of our times. Indeed, from a naive point of view, in Western society, we seem to have realized the ideals of the French Revolution, “Egalité, Fraternité, Liberté” (equality, fraternity, liberty). Woman equals man, black equals white, and children's rights are more and more being taken care of.

Closer study reveals that this equality between different animals concerns two elements: social bond and authority. Both these can be understood through Freud's study of the primal horde. The element “social bond” goes back to the fraternity, and this implies a horizontal type of relationship between equals. According to Freud, this fraternity is based on the murder of the primal father—at least in his 1913 version of Totem and Taboo. In Freud's lesser-known but more important later version in Moses and Monotheism (1939), the son will ground the fraternity on the installation of the symbolic father figure. This brings us to the second element, authority. From Freud's two versions of the myth, it is clear that authority is based on difference—more particularly, on the difference between the group of equals and the one who does not belong to this group and who, by his particular position of outsider, functions as a kind of guarantee for this group. Obviously for Freud, this position is the one taken by the father, hence his link between the primal horde and the oedipal complex.

If it is true that we are living in the era in which “all animals are equal,” this necessarily implies the obliteration of difference. In view of the fact that authority is based on difference, the implication is that authority goes down the drain as well. Unfortunately for us, the hoped-for consequences—“égalité et liberté”—fail to be realized, and we are confronted instead, at least in Europe, with an ever-increasing corporatism, racism, and nationalism. Instead of the authority of yesteryear, we meet more and more with power, which is something different.

Mark Bracher

Mark Bracher

Mark Bracher   Associate Professor in the English Department of Tsuda College. He specializes in uncovering and evaluating intersections between rhetorical and psychological theory. The Nature of Social Symptoms

In addition to material scarcity, bodily vulnerability, and human aggression, other fundamental causes of human misery are social actions, practices, institutions, and conditions that cost a society more than they contribute to its life. Such phenomena are social symptoms, and they are to the collective what Freud described “psychical symptoms” as being to the individual:

Psychical (or psychogenic) symptoms … are acts detrimental, or at least useless, to the subject's life as a whole, often complained of by him as unwelcome and bringing unpleasure and suffering to him. The main damage they do resides in the mental expenditure which they themselves involve and in the future expenditure that becomes necessary for fighting against them. Where there is an extensive formation of symptoms, these two sorts of expenditure can result in an extraordinary impoverishment of the subject in regard to the mental energy available to him and so in paralysing him for all the important tasks of life. (Lectures 358)

Social symptoms, similarly, are collective actions—including passivity, or the failure to act effectively to change undesirable but unnecessary conditions—that result in greater cost than benefit. That is, social symptoms are actions that fail to provide needed benefits even though the knowledge and material resources for providing these benefits are available. Social symptoms, then, include 1) any social problem the existence or severity of which is not inevitable, 2) any ineffective or inefficient collective attempt to solve a collective problem or meet a collective need, and 3) any other social practices, institutions, or conditions, or mass behaviors that are not inevitable and whose deleterious effects on the collectivity outweigh their benefits.

Examples of the first category include racism, sexism, and heterosexism; interpersonal, intergroup, and international violence; preventable deaths from certain illnesses (e.g., AIDS) and certain types of accidents (e.g., involving guns, cars, etc.); widespread addictions to substances such as alcohol, drugs, and tobacco; unsafe sex, which results in “unwanted” pregnancies and AIDS and other STDs; hunger and poverty in wealthy nations (and in all other nations to whose welfare wealthy nations are capable of contributing); the perpetuation of a tax system that results in a small minority possessing the great majority of the wealth; and an economic and political system that pays teachers between 1% and 10% of what it pays professional athletes and entertainers, that encourages oil and mineral extraction more than conservation, that supports space exploration more than home construction, and that rewards financial speculation more than production of vital goods and services. The reason such problems continue to exist is not because of material impediments to their removal, or even, in most cases, lack of knowledge about how they might be removed; in each instance, the wherewithal is available to eliminate or significantly reduce the problem, but political leaders and the general public fail to avail themselves of the available means. Nor is their persistence due solely or even primarily, as might appear to be the case, to the material benefits they provide to the dominant class; in many instances, their existence reduces the wealth of the wealthy, and in virtually all cases additional, more significant factors can also be seen to be at work.

One night, I had two dreams. In the first, my mother is telling me that I'm not as exceptionally beautiful as someone else's daughter. In the second, which is a recurring dream, I'm in Hawaii, where I've apparently been before. On an earlier trip, with the parents of a friend of mine, we went to an exceptionally beautiful beach. The recurring dream is that I'm in Hawaii, I keep going to an all right looking beach, and toward the end of the trip I realize I haven't gone to the really beautiful one. It seems that it's a bit harder to get to, and something seems to keep me from ever getting there or even telling the others with me that I really want to go. On this evening of two dreams, I awaken feeling that the first dream somehow explains the recurring one. The repetition of “exceptionally beautiful” suggests to me that the thing that blocks my desire has something to do with my mother not finding me exceptionally beautiful, not finding me as worthy as the friend's daughter. My mother's comment in the dream is not unlike one made in real life, when I was about 10 or 12. I begin to wonder why she would have said something like that to me.

I want to use this dream sequence and the questions it poses to think about an alternative way of understanding the nature of what Althusser, Butler, and others speak of as subjection. The question I want to pose is the following: is it useful to assume, as so much poststructuralist theory does, that subjection is inextricably linked to subject formation? The notion that subjection occurs at the same moment as subject formation suggests that subjection is the universal price paid for being a subject. Some argue that subjection is the price we pay for accession to language; Silverman, for example, speaks of the move from being into meaning. Often this move is described in terms that suggest we all suffer some kind of fall from grace, some irretrievable loss that we vainly try to make good. In so trying, the theory goes, we become hurtful to ourselves and others. The problem with such accounts is their assumption that we all suffer from the same thing. They remind me of what Barthes calls bourgeois “exnomination”: the way that dominant ideology works to make people think there are no class (or gender or race) distinctions. The people I see in my clinical practice suffer far more from the injuries of gender, race, class, and sex hierarchies than from their fall into language (or, rather, they fall into language differently depending on their place in socio-historically specific cultural hierarchies).

Capitalism, Psychic Immiseration, and Decentred Subjectivity1

Kathryn Dean

Kathryn Dean

Kathryn Dean   Lectures in social theory at the School of Oriental and African Studies, University of London. Her current research projects involve the investigation of the subject effects of different modes of communication, and the development of a psychoanalytic-Marxist theory of collective action.

Introduction

My purpose in this paper is to offer a critical realist account of decentred subjectivity. Decentred subjectivity is a specific kind of volatile subjectity which has been valorised by various postmodern writers since the late 1960s on the grounds that decentredness represents an escape from the oppressive kind of fixity attempted by the totalising discourses of the European Enlightenment.2 Where the latter have been successfully instituted, subjects in a real state of uncentredness have apparently misperceived themselves as centred and this misperception has facilitated their manipulation or oppression. Therefore to aid in the decentring of the apparently centred subject is to engage in emancipatory politics. From this point of view, modernity is a state of illusory enlightenment in which subjects conceive of themselves as centred, originary, constitutive; postmodernity is a state of true enlightenment in which subjects become aware of this illusion and refuse to accept the false comforts of the Enlightenment metanarrative. Here decentredness as a state of radical groundlessness is held to be a constitutive or innate characteristic of human life. In what follows, I want to challenge this naturalising view by offering a critical realist analysis informed by a distinction between real human causal powers and the cultural conditions needed for their actualisation (Bhaskar).3 This analysis, which is intended to reveal both the historicocultural specificity and impoverishing effects of decentredness, is made possible through the articulation of Freudian psychoanalysis and Marxian Marxism.

Arguments about decentredness and subjectivity have impinged on Marxism through the work of Althusser, in which we find an awareness of the theoretical and political importance of subjectivity and an attempt to theorise this through the articulation of psychoanalysis to Marxism (Althusser, Essays). Unfortunately, the development of this element of Althusser's work was undertaken by Laclau and Mouffe (Hegemony) whose polemics against a very crude orthodox Marxism appeared to blind Marxists to the theoretical fruitfulness of parts of this work (Geras, Discourses; Wood). The argument that follows is informed by these works in the dual sense that it both benefits from their insights and conceptual developments and attempts also to learn from their mistakes. The benefits derive from the attempt to formulate a theoretical language capable of theorizing the “social” and “psyche” relation, which, as Althusser quite rightly pointed out, is one of crucial concern to practicing Marxists. The mistakes include a failure to theorise the novelty of capitalism as culture, or total way of life, and to theorise conceptual borrowings from psychoanalysis. This failure leads to the naturalisation of decentredness. In order to rectify these mistakes, it is necessary to develop a more clearly specified and historically informed account of the conditions which constitute decentredness so as to show that this condition is not somehow the “real” or “essential” condition of humanity and second, to return to the work of Freud so as to show that decentredness is not, in any case, a condition to be celebrated but rather a state of psychic immiseration of the kind first explored by Marx in On the Jewish Question. While Marx was acutely aware of the political significance of this psychic immiseration, he did not have at his disposal the theoretical means of thinking it further and, perhaps for this reason, assumed too hastily that the condition would be transcended by means of capitalism's own developmental needs (Poverty 168; Marx and Engels, Communist).4 An understanding of the non-arrival of this transcendence requires attentiveness to the matter of subjectivity as well as of class—hence the importance of psychoanalysis to Marxism.

Modernity, Postmodernity, and Adolescence

Dany-Robert Dufour

Dany-Robert Dufour

Dany-Robert Dufour   Philosopher, a writer, and a professor of philosophy, esthetics, and education at the University of Paris VIII (Vincennes at Saint-Denis). His books include Le Bégaiement des Maîtres, Les Mystères de la Trinité, Folie et Démocratie, Lettre sur la Nature Humaine, and Being Human: The Technological Extensions of the Body (coauthored).

Modernity—and its procession of cultural and societal crises—is already a very old question: it is enough to open the most minor textbook of the history of ideas to know that modernity goes back to the times of the discovery of America. That is the historic moment when the West in a sense came out of itself and began to launch itself on an indefatigable search to outdo itself. Modern times open with this moment when everything shifted and an upheaval occurred in civilization, based on a way of life that was articulated on permanent change in all areas: technical, scientific, political, aesthetic, philosophical, etc. Since then, nothing has resisted this conquering way of life, destined to destroy all the old values, rites, and social habits, even when it led to a feeling of instability, permanent crisis, and tensions in subjectivity, and of recurring “uneasiness with civilization” (Freud), to which the younger generations, who are coming into in an extremely unstable world, are particularly sensitive.

Modernity is certainly already ancient, five centuries old, but it proved necessary to wait for the middle of the nineteenth century to notice it. It took the poet to name the new course followed by the vessel upon which humanity had embarked, to perceive this drift of civilization, or more, civilization as a drift : it was Baudelaire who invented the term “modernity” and who described, in Aesthetic Curiosities, the new subject: “So he goes, he runs, he looks. What does he look for? Certainly, this man, such as I depicted him, this solitary person endowed with an active imagination, always traveling through the great desert of people, has a purpose higher than that of a pure stroller, a more general purpose, other than the fleeting pleasure of the circumstance. He looks for something we could call modernity.” One suspects, according to this definition, that this “solitary person” may forever run, looking for modernity, without catching up with it because it is in a sense defined as overtaking itself, as the permanent questioning of its own foundations. And, indeed, modernity is that which affects everything. It is enough to consider the last hundred years to notice that nothing, including the greatest works of mind, was left untouched by it: values in philosophy, genre in literature, the metrics of verse in poetry, harmony in music, perspective and representation in painting, the foundations of language, logic and mathematics, the stable structure of space-time in the universe, and even the fixedness of the subject at the center of the world and of itself in physics, metaphysics, ontology and psychology.

Robert Samuels

Robert Samuels

Robert Samuels   Received his Doctorate in Psychoanalysis from the University of Paris VIII. He is currently teaching writing at the University of California at Santa Barbara. The first problem that one encounters in trying to articulate Lacan's theory of recognition and relate it to the question of school violence is that there is no single theory of recognition in Lacan. In fact, as is the case with most of Lacan's “theories,” the concept of recognition must be related both to the separate realms of the real, the imaginary, and the symbolic, and to the different stages of Lacan's thought. Lacan's first theory of recognition is tied to his phenomenological analysis of the ego in the 1950s. According to his early conception of the mirror stage, this ego comes into being by mis-recognizing itself in the ideal image of the other or in a reflected mirroring representation. This “imaginary” model of recognition is considered to be a mis-recognition because the subject identifies with a unified and totalized body image that is in contradiction with the subject's real sense of bodily fragmentation and lack of coordination. Moreover, Lacan claims that the subject will seek out in all of his or her objects this same imaginary level of ideal unity and comprehension. In this sense, one's ideal body image is matched by one's ideal body of knowledge. Further complicating this scenario is the fact that Lacan uses this same theory of imaginary mis-recognition to explain both the Freudian notion of narcissism and the primary relationship between the child and the mother. The theory of narcissistic recognition affirms that the subject falls in love with the ideal image that he or she sees in the other. Furthermore, the narcissistic subject is completely defined by the recognition that he or she receives from this other. In order to account for this dual task of recognition and idealization, Lacan expands the theory of the mirror stage to include both the ideal ego (the ideal image in the mirror) and the ego ideal (the Other who recognizes the subject's ideal image).

The classic illustration of this second version of the mirror stage is the child who looks into the mirror and see his own perfect image (ideal ego) and then looks back at his mother (ego ideal) who is holding him up in order to see if she recognizes his narcissistic perfection. However, this illustration is a structure that introduces into the imaginary scene a symbolic element of recognition. For the verifying mother also represents the social affirmation of the subject's sense of self. In other terms, the original role of the mother to recognize the subject's own imaginary mis-recognitions of his or her self ideal will be taken over by the symbolic functions of culture and society. This theory echoes Freud's notion that the parental ego ideal is transformed into the cultural superego through a process of internalization and symbolization.
